planting.note: Direct sow or set out transplants in spring into thin, gritty, fast-draining soil atop or alongside sandstone rock; this species is a narrow endemic of exposed sandstone outcrops on the Cumberland Plateau of northeastern Alabama and resents heavy or constantly moist soil.

directions: Grow in shallow, rocky, acidic sand or thin soil pockets over sandstone bedrock with excellent drainage and full sun exposure, mimicking the open outcrop habitat of Alabama's Cumberland Plateau where it naturally occurs. Plants form a basal perennial clump and send up wiry stems topped with gold ray flowers surrounding a reddish-brown disc from early summer into fall; deadhead spent heads to extend bloom and avoid rich or regularly irrigated garden beds, which cause lanky growth and rot. Because its range is restricted to a handful of sandstone-glade sites, this coneflower relative is best suited to rock-garden or glade-style plantings rather than conventional perennial borders.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)
